content:
TENS (Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation) machines are one of the most popular drug-free pain relief options for arthritis in the UK. These small, battery-powered devices deliver mild electrical impulses through electrode pads placed on the skin near painful joints. With prices starting from just £15 and no prescription needed, TENS machines are accessible and widely used — but do they actually work for arthritis? This guide examines the evidence, explains how to use one effectively and helps you choose the right device.

Quick answer: TENS machines are drug-free devices that deliver mild electrical impulses through pads on the skin, a popular choice for arthritis pain relief. They work by stimulating nerves to "close the gate" on pain signals (high frequency, 80-120 Hz) and by triggering endorphin release (low frequency, 2-5 Hz). Evidence suggests short-term pain relief, but they are best used as part of a wider pain management plan.

How TENS Works

TENS machines work through two main mechanisms:

Gate Control Theory

At high frequencies (80–120 Hz), TENS stimulates large nerve fibres that "close the gate" on pain signals travelling to the brain. Essentially, the tingling sensation from the TENS overrides the pain signals, reducing your perception of pain. This is similar to rubbing a bumped elbow — the pressure sensation partially blocks the pain signal.

Endorphin Release

At lower frequencies (2–5 Hz), TENS triggers the release of endorphins — the body's natural painkillers. This takes longer to work (20–30 minutes) but the pain relief can last longer after the device is switched off.

What the Evidence Says

The evidence for TENS in arthritis is mixed but generally positive for short-term pain relief:

  • A Cochrane review of TENS for knee osteoarthritis found some evidence of pain reduction, though study quality was variable
  • A meta-analysis in Physiotherapy found TENS provided statistically significant pain relief for OA compared to placebo
  • NICE acknowledges TENS as an option for osteoarthritis pain management alongside other treatments
  • Many rheumatology and physiotherapy departments in the UK recommend TENS as part of multimodal pain management
  • Patient satisfaction is generally high — many users report meaningful pain relief even when clinical trial results are modest

TENS is best viewed as one tool in a pain management toolkit, not a standalone treatment. It works well alongside exercise, medication and other approaches.

How to Use a TENS Machine for Arthritis

Pad Placement

Correct electrode placement is crucial for effective pain relief:

  • Knee arthritis — Place two pads on either side of the kneecap, or one above and one below the joint
  • Hip arthritis — Place pads around the hip joint — one at the front, one at the side or back
  • Hand/wrist arthritis — Use smaller pads on either side of the painful joint
  • Shoulder arthritis — Place pads on the front and back of the shoulder, or above and below the joint
  • Spine/back arthritis — Place pads on either side of the spine at the painful level (never directly on the spine)

Settings

  • Start with a high frequency (80–100 Hz) for immediate tingling pain relief
  • Try low frequency (2–5 Hz) for deeper, endorphin-based relief
  • Increase intensity gradually until you feel a strong but comfortable tingling — it should never be painful
  • Use for 20–60 minutes per session, up to several times daily
  • Experiment with settings — what works varies between individuals

Tips for Best Results

  • Clean and dry the skin before applying pads
  • Don't place pads on broken skin, over varicose veins or near the front of the neck
  • Replace electrode pads when they lose stickiness (every 20–30 uses typically)
  • Use during activities that usually cause pain (walking, gardening, housework)
  • Try using TENS before exercise to enable more comfortable movement

Choosing a TENS Machine

Key features to consider:

  • Dual channel — Allows you to use 4 pads simultaneously for larger areas or multiple joints
  • Adjustable frequency and intensity — More control over settings for optimal relief
  • Rechargeable battery — More economical than disposable batteries
  • Pre-set programmes — Useful for beginners, with settings optimised for different pain types
  • Timer — Automatic shut-off prevents overuse

Where to Buy in the UK

  • Boots, Superdrug and Lloyds Pharmacy stock TENS machines (from £15)
  • Amazon and online retailers offer a wide range
  • Physiotherapy suppliers (e.g., TensCare, Beurer) for more advanced devices
  • Some NHS physiotherapy departments loan TENS machines for trial periods — ask your physiotherapist

Who Should Not Use TENS

  • People with pacemakers or other implanted electrical devices (unless approved by cardiologist)
  • During pregnancy (certain pad placements)
  • Over areas of reduced sensation (neuropathy)
  • On active cancer sites
  • While driving or operating machinery

TENS machines are a safe, affordable and drug-free option for arthritis pain relief. While they don't work for everyone, many people find them a valuable addition to their pain management routine. Our virtual assistant can help you with pad placement guidance for your specific joints.

This article is for general information only. Consult your GP or physiotherapist if you're unsure whether TENS is suitable for you.

Practical next steps for TENS Machines for Arthritis UK: Do They Work and How to Use Them

If you came here about TENS Machines for Arthritis UK: Do They Work and How to Use Them, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your primary care network about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Benefits conversations

Personal Independence Payment (PIP) looks at how your condition affects daily living and mobility, not the diagnosis name alone. Keep a short diary of bad days, help you need with dressing or cooking, and walking limits. Welfare rights advisers at local councils or charities can check forms before you submit them.

Work, rights and practical adjustments

Under the Equality Act 2010, employers in Great Britain should consider reasonable adjustments when arthritis has a substantial long-term effect. That can mean flexible hours, more breaks, seating, parking closer to the entrance, or software that reduces typing strain. Acas and Citizens Advice both publish plain-English guides you can take into a meeting.

Preparing for appointments

Write three priorities before you go: main symptom, functional limit (stairs, sleep, work), and the question you most need answered. Bring a current medicine list including over-the-counter products. If English is not your first language, request an interpreter when you book.

Working with NHS pathways

Most people start with GP care, community physiotherapy and self-management, with rheumatology involved when inflammatory disease is suspected or treatment needs escalate. Ask what monitoring blood tests or reviews you should expect, and who to contact between appointments if a flare escalates.

Peer support etiquette

Share what helps you without prescribing it for others. Conditions, medicines and life circumstances differ. If someone is in crisis, encourage them toward NHS 111, their GP, or emergency services rather than relying on a forum alone.

Quick questions about TENS Machines Arthritis They

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.
